content: 1. Adequate analytical equipment and certified analytical standards, solvents, reagents, and up-to-date analytical methods must be available to ensure proper testing and evaluation of pesticides. 2. Exporting governments and international organizations should actively assist developing countries by providing training for personnel, guidance on the design and conduct of trials, interpretation and evaluation of test data, and risk/benefit analysis. 3. These entities should also promote the maximum availability and use of international, regional, and national assessments and evaluations of pesticide hazards and risks by developing countries. 4. Collaboration between the pesticide industry and governments is essential for post-registration surveillance and monitoring studies to determine the environmental and health impacts of pesticides under operational conditions. 5. Reliable data collection and maintenance of statistics on health effects and pesticide poisoning incidents should be prioritized, using harmonized tools where available. Relevant data should be submitted to designated national authorities, including the Rotterdam Convention Human Health Incident Report Forms for severely hazardous pesticide formulations. 6. Pesticides must be physically segregated from other merchandise to prevent contamination or misidentification. They should be clearly marked as hazardous materials where appropriate. 7. Governments and industries should collect reliable data and maintain statistics on environmental contamination and adverse effects related to pesticides. Specific incidents should be reported, and where applicable, the Rotterdam Convention Environmental Incidents Reporting Forms should be submitted to the designated national authority. 8. A program to monitor pesticide residues in food, feed, drinking water, the environment, and habitats where pesticides have been applied should be implemented. 9. Clear and concise labeling of pesticides is essential. Products posing unacceptable risks under any use conditions should be recalled immediately, and governments must be notified. 10. Awareness and understanding among pesticide users about protecting health and the environment from adverse effects of pesticides should be raised through education and outreach. 11. Entities addressed by the Code should promote responsible dissemination of information on pesticides, their uses, risks, and alternatives, based on all available facts. 12. Quality-assurance procedures must be maintained to ensure compliance with relevant standards of purity, performance, stability, and safety. 13. Governments should introduce necessary policies and legislation to regulate pesticides throughout their lifecycle, including marketing and use, based on FAO and WHO guidelines and relevant legal instruments. 14. Legislation should be introduced to prevent the use and sale of pesticides to children, and the use of pesticides by children in work situations should be included in National Hazardous Work Lists under ILO Convention No. 182. 15. Pesticide registration schemes and infrastructures should be established to ensure that each pesticide product is registered before being made available for use. 16. Pesticide residues in food should be regulated and monitored in accordance with Codex Alimentarius recommendations. In the absence of Codex standards, national or regional standards should be used, ensuring consistency with WTO requirements to avoid technical trade barriers. 17. Governments should ensure that pesticides are packaged and labeled in accordance with FAO/WHO guidelines and relevant national or regional regulations. 18. The importation, distribution, sale, and purchase of highly hazardous pesticides may be prohibited if risk assessments indicate that risk mitigation measures or good marketing practices are insufficient to ensure safe handling. 19. Governments and industries should prevent the accumulation of excessive pesticide stocks by encouraging market-driven supply processes rather than government purchasing. 20. Pesticide subsidies or donations should not lead to excessive or unjustified use, which may divert interest from more sustainable alternatives. 21. Pesticides manufactured or formulated by subsidiary companies must meet appropriate quality requirements and standards. 22. Pesticides restricted for use by specific groups should not be knowingly supplied to unauthorized users. 23. Purchasing procedures should be established to prevent oversupply of pesticides, including requirements for storage, distribution, and disposal services in purchasing contracts. 24. Governments should prohibit the repackaging or decanting of pesticides into inappropriate containers, such as those for food or beverages, and enforce punitive measures to deter such practices. 25. Governments, with the help of the pesticide industry and multilateral cooperation, should inventory obsolete or unusable pesticide stocks and used containers, establish action plans for their disposal, and record these activities. 26. Hazardous pesticide waste should be treated and disposed of in an environmentally sound manner, complying with national, regional, and international standards, including the Basel Convention. 27. The pesticide industry, with multilateral cooperation, should assist in the environmentally sound disposal of banned or obsolete pesticides and used containers, including reuse or recycling where approved and appropriate. 28. Policies and practices should be implemented to prevent the accumulation of obsolete pesticides and used containers. 29. Governments should regulate pesticide advertising to ensure it aligns with registration conditions, including label directions and precautions, and does not promote unsafe practices. 30. Advertising should not include misleading claims about safety or efficacy, and all promotional materials should encourage users to read and follow label instructions carefully. 31. International organizations and public interest groups should highlight deviations from the Code and promote its principles and ethics. 32. The Code should be published and observed through collaborative action by all entities involved in pesticide regulation, manufacture, distribution, and use. 33. Governments, in collaboration with FAO, WHO, and UNEP, should monitor the observance of the Code and report on progress.
